text: Johnson's praise of Shakespeare is governed by one principle, and he gives it in words which leave no ambiguity: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765). The dramatists among whom Shakespeare wrote, as Johnson represents them, commonly drew men as a particular court or city had moulded them. Their persons belonged to a season; they wore its fashions, spoke the cant of a narrow circle, and were employed upon the follies of a single year. When these fashions had gone by, their power went with them; a later reader perceives in such figures little beyond the outward trappings of a time which has disappeared. Shakespeare's persons, in Johnson's account, are framed otherwise. They act and speak from passions and principles which are not confined to one country or one age; the grief of a father and the vanity of a counsellor remain what they are, whether the scene be Elsinore or London, and whether the spectator belong to Shakespeare's day or to our own. Johnson does not maintain that the plays are without the impress of their age. He maintains rather that this impress is superficial, and that under it lies the common nature of mankind. For this reason a reader ignorant of Elizabethan manners may still believe in Polonius.
